resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

The Director's own uncertainty about whether this is primarily compressive or intrinsic cord disease supports my caution about irreversible intervention before that question is answered. As no new specific finding has been argued, I hold my position that a closely monitored 3-6 month conservative trial remains a reasonable option.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with rapidly progressive myelopathy (spastic quadriparesis, upper extremity predominant, sphincter dysfunction) and MRI showing C5-6 and C6-7 cord compression with extensive intramedullary T2 hyperintensity and focal enhancement. The clinical picture is most consistent with severe cervical spondylotic myelopathy, but the enhancing lesion introduces diagnostic uncertainty for an intrinsic cord tumor, demyelinating disease, or inflammatory myelitis. Regardless of etiology, the presence of severe, progressive deficits with sphincter involvement constitutes a surgical emergency; conservative management of 3-6 months risks irreversible cord damage. I recommend urgent surgical decompression, with intraoperative biopsy for the enhancing lesion if safely accessible, after rapid exclusion of treatable medical mimics (e.g., with whole-spine MRI, basic labs, and lumbar puncture if no contraindication).
proposed_options: Urgent anterior cervical decompression (e.g., ACDF at C5-6 and C6-7 or corpectomy as indicated by compression anatomy) with intraoperative biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion.

Immediate diagnostic workup (whole-spine and brain MRI with contrast, CSF analysis, serum inflammatory/infectious markers, and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis if concern for metastatic disease) before deciding on surgery, but with a strict 24-48 hour timeframe.
Surgical biopsy of the enhancing lesion alone (posterior approach) to establish tissue diagnosis before decompression, if the lesion is suspected to be neoplastic and separate from compression.
Conservative management trial as proposed by physiatrist (not recommended due to high risk of irreversible deterioration).
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent surgical decompression combined with lesion biopsy during the same operation, after rapid exclusion of medical mimics (not delaying beyond 48 hours).
disagreement_points: I strongly disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial: severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction is a surgical emergency, and delay risks irreversible neurologic loss. The literature supports early decompression in such cases.

An enhancing intramedullary lesion should not automatically mandate primary biopsy before decompression; spondylotic compression can cause edema and enhancement, and decompression may treat both. However, if the lesion characteristics suggest tumor (e.g., mass effect, sharp margins, nodular enhancement), biopsy can be performed at the same setting.

The record lacks key details (compression direction, stenosis grade, T1/T2 signal details, presence of foraminal stenosis, cord atrophy, dynamic instability) that affect surgical approach and urgency; immediate neuroradiology review and possibly additional MRI sequences or CT myelogram are needed.

The referral indication 'open biopsy' may be based on the initial MRI; with current data, biopsy of the spinal cord carries significant risk and may be unnecessary if compression is the primary pathology. This needs clarification.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old with severe, progressive cervical myelopathy (quadriparesis and sphincter dysfunction) over two months. MRI shows C5-6 and C6-7 cord compression with extensive T2 cord signal change and C5-6 enhancement. The differential includes compressive myelopathy, intrinsic cord tumor, or inflammatory/demyelinating lesion. The presence of cord compression and progressive deficits makes surgical decompression the most defensible intervention to prevent permanent neurological injury. The enhancing lesion can be biopsied at the same time, providing diagnostic tissue. A 3-6 month conservative trial carries an unacceptable risk of further irreversible cord damage in a patient with already severe deficits and sphincter involvement. I therefore recommend urgent surgical decompression with intraoperative biopsy, but I support completing the immediate pre-operative workup (repeat contrast MRI, laboratory studies, and formal neuro-radiology review) within 24-48 hours to refine the diagnosis and rule out a primarily medical condition. If that workup strongly suggests an inflammatory or demyelinating aetiology without significant compressive component, the plan can be reconsidered, but the default should remain surgery.
